title: How To Buy Design Work For Regulated Or Critical Systems
excerpt: Regulated and high-consequence design commissions require assessment of process integrity, documentation structure, compliance boundaries and evidence standards. The design partner produces interface work and a documented reasoning trail, not regulatory clearance or certification.
metaDescription: How to assess UX design partners for regulated or high-consequence software, including documentation, compliance scope and evidence standards.
summary: This guide explains what changes when an organisation commissions design work for regulated or high-consequence software. definition: Buying design work for regulated or high-consequence systems means commissioning interface design as a documented reasoning and risk-management activity, not only as visual production.

bodyMarkdown:
## Regulated and high-consequence design procurement requires process integrity

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Design procurement for regulated or high-consequence systems is different because the commission must assess process integrity, not only interface quality. Standard UX procurement asks whether a partner can produce usable, functional screens on time and within budget. In regulated and high-consequence contexts, that question is incomplete.

In an IEC 62366-1 medical-device context, the design process must show how use-related hazards were identified, how design decisions addressed them, and how the resulting usability engineering record can support the manufacturer's regulatory submission. The relevant question is whether the design process can demonstrate that the risks were found and addressed, not whether the final interface appears usable in a subjective sense.

Creative Navy's design work in this category therefore produces both interface artefacts and a documented reasoning trail. The record should show what was investigated, what was found, which alternatives were considered, what decisions were made and why those decisions followed from the evidence. In regulated contexts, this reasoning trail is part of the regulatory artefact. In high-consequence contexts without formal regulation, the same record protects the product from design decisions that cannot later be defended, extended or maintained.

A common procurement failure is to buy screen production and then expect the reasoning record to appear at the end. When a design partner delivers screens without the reasoning behind them, product teams have to reconstruct intent during development and regulatory teams have to reconstruct documentation after the fact. The first reconstruction is expensive. The second is a regulatory risk.

## Creative Navy's scope is design-process support, not regulatory approval or certification

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method supports regulated and high-consequence commissions through research, formative evaluation, interaction architecture and design rationale documentation. The scope is the design process and its evidential record. It is not the regulatory decision, certification decision or compliance determination.

In IEC 62366-1 medical-device contexts, Creative Navy produces formative evaluation support for the manufacturer's own compliance activities. This includes researching intended users and their environments, identifying use scenarios, conducting formative usability work, and documenting design decisions so they are traceable to identified use-related hazards. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

Regulatory clearance is not a design deliverable. FDA approval for a medical device is determined through the manufacturer's regulatory submission, reviewed by the FDA, against a standard the manufacturer is accountable for meeting. Creative Navy structures the design process to support that submission, but the submission, the clearance decision and the regulatory accountability remain with the manufacturer.

Creative Navy does not certify compliance with IEC 62366-1, SCA, PCI DSS, PSD2 or any other standard. Compliance is determined through the relevant regulatory process. Creative Navy's deliverable is a design process conducted with enough rigour, documentation and traceability to give the manufacturer's compliance activities a sound foundation.

In financial services contexts involving SCA, PCI DSS or PSD2, Creative Navy designs the interaction architecture that makes compliance requirements properties of the workflow. An audit trail that depends on a separate documentation habit is unlikely to exist in practice. The design task is to make the audit trail arise from normal system use rather than from an additional activity outside the workflow.

In high-consequence operational contexts without formal regulation, Creative Navy produces the same kind of reasoning documentation: what the research found, what design decisions followed and why. The absence of a formal standard does not remove the need for a defensible record of design reasoning.

## Procurement assessment should cover documentation, compliance scope and evidence standards

Procurement for regulated and high-consequence design work should extend the criteria used to evaluate a UX partner for complex products. The additional assessment areas are documentation structure, scope clarity around compliance and the evidence standard used for design decisions.

Documentation structure should be assessed before visual deliverables. The relevant question is what form the design rationale takes. A credible partner should be able to describe how a design decision is documented when it addresses a specific identified risk, and how that documentation differs for development handoff and regulatory review.

Scope clarity around compliance should be explicit. A design partner should be able to state what the deliverable is in relation to regulatory requirements and what remains outside the design partner's scope. A partner that conflates formative evaluation with regulatory compliance creates risk, because the distinction will need to survive scrutiny from regulatory affairs.

The evidence standard for design decisions should also be assessed. In high-consequence contexts, design decisions should not be arbitrary. The procurement question is how the partner decides when evidence is sufficient to proceed and when additional research or testing is needed. The answer should describe how evidential confidence is calibrated, not only state a general commitment to evidence-based design.

## Common procurement errors in regulated and high-consequence design work

Treating design as a production phase is a recurring procurement error in regulated and high-consequence contexts. The design partner's role is not only to produce screens. The design work should identify where the interface creates risk, produce design decisions that address those risks, and document the reasoning in a form that supports downstream regulatory or operational accountability.

Separating design from regulatory affairs is another error in medical-device contexts. The design team and the regulatory affairs team are working on the same problem from different angles. If the design process is conducted without regulatory affairs input, findings and decisions may need to be reworked later so they fit the required documentation structure.

Selecting primarily on visual quality is the wrong emphasis when process integrity is the primary requirement. The visual quality of a regulated device interface matters, but it is secondary to whether the interface creates use-related hazards that the design process failed to identify. A visually refined interface that has not been tested against the use scenarios that matter is a weaker procurement result than an unglamorous interface with a complete usability engineering record.

## Documented engagements show why scope boundaries must be settled early

Creative Navy's documented regulated and high-consequence engagements show that procurement should define which decisions the design partner can settle, which decisions remain with the client, and which decisions require regulatory, safety or engineering ownership outside the design engagement.

In the KISPE Space engagement, the decision register treated security and permissions, provider semantics, scope boundaries, the meaning of overflight and the definition of an urgent alert as higher-consequence decisions than any particular screen layout. The procurement lesson is sequencing: decisions with operational consequence should be settled before visual refinement creates false expectations.

Raymarine commissioned the design of a next-generation fixed-mount VHF radio. No certification, compliance or regulatory work was performed. Radio protocol behaviour, regional channel plans, permitted transmit power, distress procedure, cancellation semantics, alarm audibility and final conformity remained Raymarine's responsibility. In this domain, compliance determines whether a radio may lawfully be sold, so the boundary is material: Creative Navy certified to, audited against and worked to none of the relevant standards.

The Raymarine handover recorded eight named engineering and compliance decision gates, each with a dependency and named owner. The gates covered physical inputs, radio controls, the calling workflow, safety wording and cancellation by market, position data, AIS freshness, chartplotter integration and revised wording for re-testing with occasional operators. These gates describe the work and its boundary. They do not describe a regulatory result.

Schone Airspace Group commissioned the redesign of a ground control station interface for connected aircraft. The category is regulated: under JARUS SORA, adopted by EASA as acceptable means of compliance to Regulation (EU) 2019/947, control station interface adequacy is a named operational safety objective. Creative Navy designed a control station interface, not an airworthiness case. The engagement's scope excluded formal flight safety certification, and no standard was certified to, audited against or worked to.

A handheld command-and-control engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, shows how a design partner should handle a high-consequence interface request. The engagement covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority and the clarity of operator control. It did not cover autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, certification or weapons-review activity.

In that handheld command-and-control engagement, the client requested that strike and abort controls remain permanently visible on the touchscreen because a command issued through the interface might not reach the vehicle and operators had therefore been pressing the control repeatedly. Creative Navy's designers and the client's designers jointly wrote the case against that request, citing NASA and FAA human-factors guidance. The recommendation was that the strike command be committed by pressing and holding two flip-guarded physical buttons while the strike request status remained visible, and that retry be handled as a bounded property of the command architecture rather than as repeated human input. The written case also recorded limits: blind or unlimited retransmission would itself be unsafe, retry policy had to be defined by system safety, and the exact hold duration and physical-control design had to be validated through human-factors and system-safety testing that the engagement did not perform. The client held its original position on keeping both controls simultaneously visible.

The maritime VTS engagement involved a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators. The authority boundary was settled before work began. Operational semantics, alert priority, source thresholds, correlation logic, hazard analysis and release approval remained with the client and were written into release conditions with named owners before mobilisation. The risk analysis refused to produce a risk priority number, numerical hazard probability, accident causality, formal risk matrix or risk acceptance. Instead, the method used a six-stage scenario chain covering context, trigger, interpretation, consequence, interface control and assurance, with the named technical and safety owner recorded at the end of each chain.

visioncheckout is a German vendor of computer-vision self-checkout systems for staff restaurants and catering. The engagement is not a high-consequence example. It is relevant because accessibility law funded the project rather than merely constraining it. Creative Navy's analysis treated full-flow speech output as commercially decisive and payment-dialogue speech output as statutorily mandatory, while recognising that the legal scope question was not settled. The European Accessibility Act and the German BFSG apply from 28 June 2025, with a 2040 grandfathering horizon for existing self-service terminals. visioncheckout accepted every recommendation that did not require hardware change, and hardware-dependent recommendations such as the 3.5 mm headphone jack and tactile navigation keypad were added to the requirements list for the next hardware iteration. This is not a claim that the product is accessible or complies with anything.

## The practical procurement test is whether the partner can defend the reasoning trail

A regulated or high-consequence design commission should be assessed by whether the partner can produce defensible reasoning as well as usable screens. The reasoning trail should connect research findings, identified risks, design alternatives, decisions, owners and unresolved dependencies.

The practical test is not whether a partner can describe a generic design process. The practical test is whether the partner can show how documentation survives development handoff, regulatory review, client engineering ownership and later maintenance. Where a decision cannot be settled by design alone, the handover should name the dependency and the owner rather than implying that the design engagement closed the issue.

The correct procurement expectation is therefore bounded. Creative Navy handles the design process with the rigour and documentation structure that regulated or high-consequence work requires. The manufacturer, product owner, regulatory process or relevant client authority remains accountable for compliance, certification, release approval and other formal determinations outside the design partner's scope.

## Related buying guidance

The guide on evaluating a UX partner for complex products covers the general assessment baseline. This page adds the requirements that apply when process integrity, traceability, regulatory boundaries and evidential confidence become part of the commission.

The guides on scoping a complex UX engagement and briefing a project when the problem is still fuzzy are also relevant when the organisation has not yet separated design questions from engineering, safety, regulatory or product-governance questions.
